claim: Unpaired ligands act via a GP130-like receptor, domeless, to activate JAK/STAT signalling in Drosophila.
source: Unpaired ligands are secreted signals that act via a GP130-like receptor, domeless, to activate JAK/STAT signalling in Drosophila.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila JAK/STAT pathway, supported by the manuscript's introduction and background.

claim: Unpaired cytokines can be activated by infection and other stresses.
source: Like many mammalian cytokines, unpaireds can be activated by infection and other stresses and can promote insulin resistance in target tissues.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about unpaired cytokine activation.

claim: Unpaired cytokines can promote insulin resistance in target tissues.
source: Like many mammalian cytokines, unpaireds can be activated by infection and other stresses and can promote insulin resistance in target tissues.
evidence: This is supported by prior research on unpaired cytokines and insulin resistance.

claim: Adult muscles show basal JAK-STAT signalling activity in the absence of any immune challenge.
source: Adult muscles show basal JAK-STAT signalling activity in the absence of any immune challenge.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the STAT-GFP reporter activity shown in Figure 1A and described in the Results section.

claim: Plasmatocytes (Drosophila macrophages) are an important source of tonic JAK-STAT signal in adult muscles.
source: Plasmatocytes (Drosophila macrophages) are an important source of this tonic signal.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing plasmatocyte depletion reduces STAT-GFP activity in muscles (Figure 4D,E).

claim: Loss of the dome receptor on adult muscles significantly reduces lifespan.
source: Loss of the dome receptor on adult muscles significantly reduces lifespan and causes local and systemic metabolic pathology.
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival curves in Figure 1B showing reduced lifespan in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.

claim: Loss of the dome receptor on adult muscles causes local and systemic metabolic pathology.
source: Loss of the dome receptor on adult muscles significantly reduces lifespan and causes local and systemic metabolic pathology.
evidence: This is supported by data showing lipid accumulation (Figure 1D), reduced metabolites (Figure 1E,F), and altered metabolic rate (Figure 1G).

claim: The pathologies resulting from dome loss in adult muscles result from hyperactivation of AKT.
source: These pathologies result from hyperactivation of AKT and consequent deregulation of metabolism.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots showing increased phospho-AKT (Figure 1H) and rescue experiments with AKT knockdown (Figure 3G).

claim: Dome signalling in muscle controls AKT activity and metabolic homeostasis.
source: Thus, we identify a cytokine signal that must be received in muscle to control AKT activity and metabolic homeostasis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by multiple experiments showing AKT hyperactivation upon dome loss and metabolic dysregulation.

claim: The strongest STAT-responsive GFP reporter activity in adult flies was observed in legs and thorax.
source: The strongest reporter activity we observed was in legs and thorax.
evidence: This is based on observation of the 10xSTAT92E-GFP reporter described in the Results section.

claim: STAT-GFP and muscle MHC-RFP expression co-localize in muscles of legs, thorax and body wall.
source: We examined flies also carrying a muscle myosin heavy chain RFP reporter (MHC-RFP) and observed co-localization of GFP and RFP expression in the muscles of the legs, thorax and body wall (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy images showing co-localization in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: STAT reporter expression is strong in various leg and jump muscles and apparently weaker in body wall muscles and indirect flight muscles.
source: We observed strong, somewhat heterogeneous reporter expression in all the muscles of the thorax and the legs, with strong expression in various leg and jump muscles and apparently weaker expression throughout the body wall muscles and indirect flight muscles (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on visual observation of the STAT-GFP reporter shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Flies with Dome signalling inhibited in adult muscles were short-lived.
source: Flies with Dome signalling inhibited in adult muscles were short-lived (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival curves in Figure 1B showing significantly reduced lifespan.

claim: The lifespan reduction effect of dome inhibition was also observed, more weakly, in flies kept at 25°C.
source: This effect was also observed, more weakly, in flies kept at 25°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D with survival curves at 25°C.

claim: Upd-JAK-STAT signalling is important to maintain gut integrity.
source: Upd-JAK-STAT signalling is important to maintain gut integrity, and defects in gut integrity often precede death in Drosophila; however, our flies did not exhibit loss of gut integrity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Jiang et al., 2009; Rera et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior publications (Jiang et al., 2009; Rera et al., 2012).

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies did not exhibit loss of gut integrity.
source: Upd-JAK-STAT signalling is important to maintain gut integrity, and defects in gut integrity often precede death in Drosophila; however, our flies did not exhibit loss of gut integrity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Jiang et al., 2009; Rera et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Smurf assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies showed significantly impaired climbing compared to controls.
source: 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies showed significantly impaired climbing compared to controls (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by negative geotaxis assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Adult muscle-specific expression of domeΔ with Mef2-Gal4 gave a similar reduction in lifespan and decline in climbing activity.
source: Adult muscle-specific expression of domeΔ with a second Gal4 line (w;tub-Gal80ts;Mef2-Gal4) gave a similar reduction in lifespan and decline in climbing activity, confirming that the defect resulted from a requirement for Dome activity in muscle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival and climbing data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Impaired muscle function is sometimes accompanied by lipid accumulation.
source: Impaired muscle function is sometimes accompanied by lipid accumulation (Baik et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Baik et al., 2017).

claim: Numerous small neutral lipid inclusions were detected in several muscles, including the large jump muscle (TTM), of 14 day old 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.
source: In 14 day old flies, we detected numerous small neutral lipid inclusions in several muscles, including the large jump muscle (TTM), of 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LipidTox staining shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies showed significant reductions in total triglyceride.
source: We observed significant reductions in total triglyceride, glycogen and free sugar (glucose + trehalose) in these animals (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TLC analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies showed significant reductions in glycogen.
source: We observed significant reductions in total triglyceride, glycogen and free sugar (glucose + trehalose) in these animals (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by glycogen measurements in Figure 1F.

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies showed significant reductions in free sugar (glucose + trehalose).
source: We observed significant reductions in total triglyceride, glycogen and free sugar (glucose + trehalose) in these animals (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by glucose and trehalose measurements in Figure 1F.

claim: CO2 production was significantly increased in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.
source: CO2 production and O2 consumption were both significantly increased in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies, indicating an overall increase in metabolic rate (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by respirometry data in Figure 1G.

claim: O2 consumption was significantly increased in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.
source: CO2 production and O2 consumption were both significantly increased in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies, indicating an overall increase in metabolic rate (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by respirometry data in Figure 1G.

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies showed an overall increase in metabolic rate.
source: CO2 production and O2 consumption were both significantly increased in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies, indicating an overall increase in metabolic rate (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is inferred from the increased CO2 production and O2 consumption shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Insulin signalling via AKT is the primary driver of sugar uptake by peripheral tissues.
source: Of these, insulin signalling via AKT is the primary driver of sugar uptake by peripheral tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insulin signaling and glucose uptake.

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies showed an extremely strong increase in abundance of the 60 kDa form of total and activated (S505-phosphorylated) AKT.
source: We found an extremely strong increase in abundance of the 60 kDa form of total and activated (S505-phosphorylated) AKT (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 1H,I.

claim: The increase in AKT abundance was also seen in legs from Mef2-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.
source: This change was also seen in legs from Mef2-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies, confirming that dome functions in muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H,I.

claim: The AKT hyperactivation effect was also seen in MHC-Gal4 >dome∆ (II) flies, though the effect was weaker.
source: We also saw this effect in flies carrying a different insertion of the dome∆ transgene, under the control of a third muscle-specific driver, MHC-Gal4, though the effect was weaker; the weakness of this effect may be a consequence of the fact that the MHC-Gal4 driver is not expressed in visceral muscle (Bland et al., 2010) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and cited from Bland et al., 2010.

claim: MHC-Gal4 >dome∆ (II) animals were short-lived relative to controls.
source: These MHC-Gal4 >dome∆ (II) animals were also short-lived relative to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Akt1 transcript levels were elevated in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ muscle by about 75%.
source: We distinguished between these possibilities by assaying Akt1 mRNA; Akt1 transcript levels were elevated in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ muscle, but only by about 75%, suggesting that the large effect on AKT protein abundance must be, at least in part, post-transcriptional (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1L.

claim: The large effect on AKT protein abundance must be, at least in part, post-transcriptional.
source: We distinguished between these possibilities by assaying Akt1 mRNA; Akt1 transcript levels were elevated in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ muscle, but only by about 75%, suggesting that the large effect on AKT protein abundance must be, at least in part, post-transcriptional (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between the 75% increase in mRNA and the much larger increase in protein.

claim: None of the insulin-like peptides Ilp2-7 were significantly overexpressed in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.
source: Similarly, AKT hyperactivation could be driven by insulin-like peptide overexpression; however, we assayed the expression of Ilp2-7 in whole flies and observed that none of these peptides were significantly overexpressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1M-R.

claim: Food uptake was not different in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies compared to controls.
source: Next, we analysed if the feeding behaviour is affected by the muscle-specific dome loss, but we could not find a difference in food uptake in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by feeding assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1S.

claim: The amino-acid-responsive TORC1/S6K pathway showed no significant difference in activity in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.
source: Unlike AKT, the amino-acid-responsive TORC1/S6K and the starvation-responsive AMPK pathway showed no significant difference in activity in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies (Figure 1K,L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis of phospho-p70 S6K in Figure 1J.

claim: The starvation-responsive AMPK pathway showed no significant difference in activity in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.
source: Unlike AKT, the amino-acid-responsive TORC1/S6K and the starvation-responsive AMPK pathway showed no significant difference in activity in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies (Figure 1K,L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis of phospho-AMPKα in Figure 1K.

claim: Flies with AMPK knocked down in muscle exhibited mild AKT hyperactivation.
source: However, flies with AMPK knocked down in muscle did exhibit mild AKT hyperactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was an insignificant reduction in ERK activity in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.
source: We found an insignificant reduction in ERK activity in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis of phospho-ERK in Figure 1L.

claim: rl and Dsor1 knockdown gave mild or no effect on survival and pAKT.
source: rl and Dsor1 knockdown gave mild or no effect on survival and pAKT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot and survival data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: hop knockdown gave a mild phenocopy of dome∆ with regards to survival and pAKT.
source: In contrast, hop knockdown gave a mild phenocopy of dome∆ with regards to survival and pAKT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot and survival data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Flies carrying hopTum-l alone exhibited no change in lifespan.
source: Flies carrying hopTum-l alone exhibited no change in lifespan, AKT phosphorylation, or muscle lipid deposition (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data in Figure 2A.

claim: Flies carrying hopTum-l alone exhibited no change in AKT phosphorylation.
source: Flies carrying hopTum-l alone exhibited no change in lifespan, AKT phosphorylation, or muscle lipid deposition (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 2B.

claim: Flies carrying hopTum-l alone exhibited no change in muscle lipid deposition.
source: Flies carrying hopTum-l alone exhibited no change in lifespan, AKT phosphorylation, or muscle lipid deposition (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LipidTox staining in Figure 2C.

claim: hopTum-l completely rescued lifespan in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.
source: However, hopTum-l completely rescued lifespan and pAKT levels in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies (Figure 2D,E), indicating that the physiological activity of muscle Dome is mediated via Hop and that signal is required, but not sufficient, to control muscle AKT activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data in Figure 2D.

claim: hopTum-l completely rescued pAKT levels in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.
source: However, hopTum-l completely rescued lifespan and pAKT levels in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies (Figure 2D,E), indicating that the physiological activity of muscle Dome is mediated via Hop and that signal is required, but not sufficient, to control muscle AKT activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 2E.

claim: The physiological activity of muscle Dome is mediated via Hop.
source: However, hopTum-l completely rescued lifespan and pAKT levels in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies (Figure 2D,E), indicating that the physiological activity of muscle Dome is mediated via Hop and that signal is required, but not sufficient, to control muscle AKT activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments showing hopTum-l rescues the dome∆ phenotype.

claim: Hop signal is required, but not sufficient, to control muscle AKT activity.
source: However, hopTum-l completely rescued lifespan and pAKT levels in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies (Figure 2D,E), indicating that the physiological activity of muscle Dome is mediated via Hop and that signal is required, but not sufficient, to control muscle AKT activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that hopTum-l alone does not change AKT levels but rescues the dome∆ phenotype.

claim: The phenotype of 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies is similar to that previously described in flies with loss of function in Pten or foxo.
source: The phenotype of 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies is similar to that previously described in flies with loss of function in Pten or foxo (Demontis and Perrimon, 2010; Mensah et al., 2015), suggesting that AKT hyperactivation might cause the dome loss of function phenotype; however, to our knowledge, direct activation of muscle AKT had not previously been analysed.
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior published work (Demontis and Perrimon, 2010; Mensah et al., 2015).

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > myr-AKT flies phenocopied 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies with regards to lifespan.
source: These animals phenocopied 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies with regards to lifespan, climbing activity, metabolite levels, metabolic rate, and muscle lipid deposition (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data in Figure 3A.

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > myr-AKT flies phenocopied 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies with regards to climbing activity.
source: These animals phenocopied 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies with regards to lifespan, climbing activity, metabolite levels, metabolic rate, and muscle lipid deposition (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by negative geotaxis assay data in Figure 3B.

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > myr-AKT flies phenocopied 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies with regards to metabolite levels.
source: These animals phenocopied 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies with regards to lifespan, climbing activity, metabolite levels, metabolic rate, and muscle lipid deposition (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TLC and metabolite measurements in Figure 3C,D.

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > myr-AKT flies phenocopied 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies with regards to metabolic rate.
source: These animals phenocopied 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies with regards to lifespan, climbing activity, metabolite levels, metabolic rate, and muscle lipid deposition (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by respirometry data in Figure 3E.

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > myr-AKT flies phenocopied 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies with regards to muscle lipid deposition.
source: These animals phenocopied 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies with regards to lifespan, climbing activity, metabolite levels, metabolic rate, and muscle lipid deposition (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LipidTox staining in Figure 3F.

claim: Flies carrying muscle-specific inducible dominant negative dome with dsRNA against Akt1 showed significantly longer lifespan than 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies.
source: We generated flies carrying muscle-specific inducible dominant negative dome (UAS-dome∆) with dsRNA against Akt1 (UAS-AKT-IR). These flies showed significantly longer lifespan than 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ and 24B-Gal80ts > AKT IR flies, similar to all control genotypes analyzed (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data in Figure 3G.

claim: Dome and AKT antagonism synergised to control the mRNA level of dome itself.
source: Dome and AKT antagonism synergised to control the mRNA level of dome itself, further suggesting strong mutual antagonism between these pathways (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Combining 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ with a foxo-GFP transgene exhibited rescue of physiological defects and lifespan.
source: To test whether this loss of FOXO activity caused some of the pathologies observed in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies, we increased foxo gene dosage by combining 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ with a transgene carrying a FOXO-GFP fusion protein under the control of the endogenous foxo regulatory regions. These animals exhibited rescue of physiological defects and lifespan compared to 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies (Figure 3H–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival and metabolite data in Figure 3H-J.

claim: foxoGFP;24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies exhibited increased dome expression.
source: They also exhibited increased dome expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Dome blockade increased upd2 expression.
source: The strongest effect we observed was that Dome blockade increased upd2 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the observation that FOXO activity inhibits upd2 expression in muscle (none of the other genes tested have been shown to be FOXO targets in muscle) (Zhao and Karpac, 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and cited from Zhao and Karpac, 2017.

claim: FOXO activity inhibits upd2 expression in muscle.
source: The strongest effect we observed was that Dome blockade increased upd2 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the observation that FOXO activity inhibits upd2 expression in muscle (none of the other genes tested have been shown to be FOXO targets in muscle) (Zhao and Karpac, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Zhao and Karpac, 2017).

claim: 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ markedly increased FOXO-GFP abundance.
source: We found that 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ markedly increased FOXO-GFP abundance, so that the increase in total FOXO was much greater than 1.5-fold (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The increase in FOXO-GFP drove an apparent feedback effect, restoring AKT in leg samples of foxoGFP;24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies to near-normal levels.
source: This drove an apparent feedback effect, restoring AKT in leg samples of foxoGFP;24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ flies to near-normal levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: No clear regulation of Akh itself was observed in 24B-Gal80ts > dome∆ animals.
source: We observed no clear regulation of Akh itself or of Hsl, bmm, or plin2; plin1 was reduced in expression by expression of dome∆.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: plin1 was reduced in expression by expression of dome∆.
source: We observed no clear regulation of Akh itself or of Hsl, bmm, or plin2; plin1 was reduced in expression by expression of dome∆.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L.

claim: The primary effect of muscle dome is on AKT-foxo signalling.
source: We conclude that the primary effect of muscle dome is on AKT-foxo signalling.
evidence: This is inferred from the various experiments showing effects on AKT and FOXO but not other pathways.

claim: Plasmatocytes are a key source of upd3 in flies on high fat diet.
source: Plasmatocytes—Drosophila macrophages—are a key source of upd3 in flies on high fat diet and in mycobacterial infection (Péan et al., 2017; Woodcock et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Péan et al., 2017; Woodcock et al., 2015).

claim: Plasmatocytes are a key source of upd3 in mycobacterial infection.
source: Plasmatocytes—Drosophila macrophages—are a key source of upd3 in flies on high fat diet and in mycobacterial infection (Péan et al., 2017; Woodcock et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Péan et al., 2017; Woodcock et al., 2015).

claim: Plasmatocytes express upd1-3 in unchallenged flies.
source: Plasmatocytes also express upd1-3 in unchallenged flies (Chakrabarti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Chakrabarti et al., 2016).

claim: Plasmatocytes were found close to STAT-GFP-positive leg muscle.
source: We found plasmatocytes close to STAT-GFP-positive leg muscle (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy images in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Overexpression of upd3 in plasmatocytes caused a potent increase in muscle STAT-GFP activity.
source: We then overexpressed upd3 in plasmatocytes and observed a potent increase in muscle STAT-GFP activity (Figure 4C), confirming that plasmatocyte-derived upd signals were able to activate muscle Dome.
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification in Figure 4C.

claim: Plasmatocyte-derived upd signals are able to activate muscle Dome.
source: We then overexpressed upd3 in plasmatocytes and observed a potent increase in muscle STAT-GFP activity (Figure 4C), confirming that plasmatocyte-derived upd signals were able to activate muscle Dome.
evidence: This is inferred from the upd3 overexpression experiment showing increased muscle STAT-GFP.

claim: Plasmatocyte-depleted flies exhibited a near-complete elimination of plasmatocytes within 24 hr of being shifted to 29°C.
source: These animals exhibited a near-complete elimination of plasmatocytes within 24 hr of being shifted to 29°C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging and flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: STAT-GFP fluorescence was reduced in legs of plasmatocyte-depleted flies compared to controls.
source: STAT-GFP fluorescence and GFP abundance were reduced in legs of plasmatocyte-depleted flies (crq-Gal80ts > rpr) compared to controls (crq-Gal80ts/+) (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy in Figure 4D.

claim: GFP abundance was reduced in legs of plasmatocyte-depleted flies compared to controls.
source: STAT-GFP fluorescence and GFP abundance were reduced in legs of plasmatocyte-depleted flies (crq-Gal80ts > rpr) compared to controls (crq-Gal80ts/+) (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 4E.

claim: STAT-GFP activity was not eliminated in plasmatocyte-depleted flies, indicating that plasmatocytes are not the only source of muscle STAT-activating signals.
source: Activity was not eliminated, indicating that plasmatocytes are not the only source of muscle STAT-activating signals, although these animals did exhibit a significant reduction in climbing activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that STAT-GFP activity is reduced but not eliminated in plasmatocyte-depleted flies.

claim: Plasmatocyte-depleted flies exhibited a significant reduction in climbing activity.
source: Activity was not eliminated, indicating that plasmatocytes are not the only source of muscle STAT-activating signals, although these animals did exhibit a significant reduction in climbing activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by negative geotaxis assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Plasmatocyte depletion resulted in short-lived flies.
source: Plasmatocyte depletion gave animals that were short-lived (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data in Figure 4F.

claim: Combining plasmatocyte depletion with null mutations in upd2 and upd3 did not significantly further reduce lifespan.
source: Combining plasmatocyte depletion with null mutations in upd2 and upd3 did not significantly further reduce lifespan; upd2 upd3 mutants with plamatocytes intact exhibited near-normal lifespan (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data in Figure 4F.

claim: upd2 upd3 mutants with plasmatocytes intact exhibited near-normal lifespan.
source: Combining plasmatocyte depletion with null mutations in upd2 and upd3 did not significantly further reduce lifespan; upd2 upd3 mutants with plamatocytes intact exhibited near-normal lifespan (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data in Figure 4F.

claim: Plasmatocyte depletion drove muscle lipid accumulation.
source: Similarly, plasmatocyte depletion drove muscle lipid accumulation, and upd2 upd3 mutation synergised with plasmatocyte depletion to further increase muscle lipid inclusions (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LipidTox staining in Figure 4G.

claim: upd2 upd3 mutation synergised with plasmatocyte depletion to further increase muscle lipid inclusions.
source: Similarly, plasmatocyte depletion drove muscle lipid accumulation, and upd2 upd3 mutation synergised with plasmatocyte depletion to further increase muscle lipid inclusions (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LipidTox staining in Figure 4G.

claim: Plasmatocyte depletion reduced free sugar levels in the whole fly.
source: Plasmatocyte depletion reduced free sugar levels as well as glycogen levels in the whole fly (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), but did not reduce the abundance of stored triglycerides (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolite measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Plasmatocyte depletion reduced glycogen levels in the whole fly.
source: Plasmatocyte depletion reduced free sugar levels as well as glycogen levels in the whole fly (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), but did not reduce the abundance of stored triglycerides (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolite measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Plasmatocyte depletion did not reduce the abundance of stored triglycerides.
source: Plasmatocyte depletion reduced free sugar levels as well as glycogen levels in the whole fly (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), but did not reduce the abundance of stored triglycerides (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TLC analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Depleting plasmatocytes in upd2 upd3 mutants failed to recapitulate the effects of muscle Dome inhibition on whole-animal triglyceride, free sugar, and glycogen levels.
source: However, depleting plasmatocytes in upd2 upd3 mutants failed to recapitulate the effects of muscle Dome inhibition on whole-animal triglyceride, free sugar, and glycogen levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metabolite measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: upd2 upd3 double-mutants were apparently normal with regards to STAT-GFP activity.
source: However, these mutants, including the upd2 upd3 double-mutant, were apparently normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Plasmatocyte-specific knockdown of upd1 and upd3 resulted in essentially normal flies.
source: We then tested plasmatocyte-specific knockdown of upd1 and upd3; these animals were also essentially normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and plasmatocyte upd1 knockdown did not reduce lifespan (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging and Western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: Plasmatocyte upd1 knockdown did not reduce lifespan.
source: We then tested plasmatocyte-specific knockdown of upd1 and upd3; these animals were also essentially normal (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and plasmatocyte upd1 knockdown did not reduce lifespan (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data in Figure 4H.

claim: Plasmatocyte-specific upd1 knockdown gave significant compensating increases in expression of upd2 and upd3.
source: However, plasmatocyte-specific upd1 knockdown gave significant compensating increases in expression of upd2 and upd3 (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4I.

claim: Combining plasmatocyte-specific upd1 knockdown with mutations in upd2 and upd3 reduced lifespan.
source: In keeping with this, combining plasmatocyte-specific upd1 knockdown with mutations in upd2 and upd3 reduced lifespan (Figure 4J) and also reduced STAT-GFP activity in these flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data in Figure 4J.

claim: Combining plasmatocyte-specific upd1 knockdown with mutations in upd2 and upd3 reduced STAT-GFP activity.
source: In keeping with this, combining plasmatocyte-specific upd1 knockdown with mutations in upd2 and upd3 reduced lifespan (Figure 4J) and also reduced STAT-GFP activity in these flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Plasmatocytes are an important physiological source of the Upd signal driving muscle Dome activity in healthy flies.
source: Our results indicate that plasmatocytes are an important physiological source of the Upd signal driving muscle Dome activity in healthy flies, and suggest that upd1 may be the primary relevant signal in healthy animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the various experiments showing plasmatocyte depletion reduces muscle STAT activity and affects lifespan.

claim: upd1 may be the primary relevant signal from plasmatocytes in healthy animals.
source: Our results indicate that plasmatocytes are an important physiological source of the Upd signal driving muscle Dome activity in healthy flies, and suggest that upd1 may be the primary relevant signal in healthy animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the compensatory upregulation of upd2 and upd3 when upd1 is knocked down, and the effects of triple knockdown/mutation.

claim: Plasmatocytes are not the only relevant source of Upd signal for muscle Dome activity.
source: However, plasmatocytes are not the only relevant source of signal, and Upd mutual regulation prevents us from pinpointing a single responsible signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that STAT-GFP activity is not completely eliminated in plasmatocyte-depleted flies.

claim: upd-dome signalling in muscle acts via AKT to regulate physiological homeostasis in Drosophila.
source: Here we show that upd-dome signalling in muscle acts via AKT to regulate physiological homeostasis in Drosophila.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experiments throughout.

claim: Loss of Dome activity in adult muscles shortens lifespan and promotes local and systemic metabolic disruption.
source: Loss of Dome activity in adult muscles shortens lifespan and promotes local and systemic metabolic disruption.
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data (Figure 1B) and metabolic measurements (Figure 1D-G).

claim: Dome specifically regulates the level and activity of AKT.
source: Dome specifically regulates the level and activity of AKT; AKT hyper-activation mediates the observed pathology.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blots showing AKT hyperactivation (Figure 1H,I) and lack of effects on other pathways (Figure 1J,K,L).

claim: AKT hyper-activation mediates the observed pathology in dome loss-of-function flies.
source: Dome specifically regulates the level and activity of AKT; AKT hyper-activation mediates the observed pathology.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phenocopy with myr-AKT expression (Figure 3A-F) and rescue with AKT knockdown (Figure 3G).

claim: In healthy adult flies, insulin-like peptides are the primary physiological AKT agonists.
source: In healthy adult flies, insulin-like peptides are the primary physiological AKT agonists.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insulin signaling in Drosophila.

claim: The effect observed is an example of a cytokine-Dome-JAK signal that impairs insulin function to permit healthy physiology.
source: The effect we observe thus appears to be an example of a cytokine-Dome-JAK signal that impairs insulin function to permit healthy physiology.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of Dome leads to AKT hyperactivation and pathology.

claim: Upd1 acts locally in the brain to regulate feeding and energy storage by altering the secretion of neuropeptide F (NPF).
source: Upd1 acts locally in the brain to regulate feeding and energy storage by altering the secretion of neuropeptide F (NPF) (Beshel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Beshel et al., 2017).

claim: Upd2 is released by the fat body in response to dietary triglyceride and sugar to regulate secretion of insulin-like peptides.
source: Upd2 is released by the fat body in response to dietary triglyceride and sugar to regulate secretion of insulin-like peptides (Rajan and Perrimon, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Rajan and Perrimon, 2012).

claim: Muscle-derived Upd2, under control of FOXO, regulates production of the glucagon-like signal Akh.
source: More recently, muscle-derived Upd2, under control of FOXO, has been shown to regulate production of the glucagon-like signal Akh (Zhao and Karpac, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Zhao and Karpac, 2017).

claim: Plasmatocyte-derived Upd3 in flies on a high fat diet can activate the JAK/STAT pathway in various organs including muscles and can promote insulin insensitivity.
source: Plasmatocyte-derived Upd3 in flies on a high fat diet can activate the JAK/STAT pathway in various organs including muscles and can promote insulin insensitivity (Woodcock et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Woodcock et al., 2015).

claim: In larvae, muscle JAK/STAT signalling loss of function results in reduced AKT activity.
source: In larvae, muscle JAK/STAT signalling can have an effect opposite to the one we report, with pathway loss of function resulting in reduced AKT activity (Yang and Hultmark, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Yang and Hultmark, 2017).

claim: JAK/STAT signalling in adult visceral muscle regulates expression of Vein, an EGF-family ligand, to control intestinal stem cell proliferation.
source: Roles in specific muscle populations have also been described: for example, JAK/STAT signalling in adult visceral muscle regulates expression of Vein, an EGF-family ligand, to control intestinal stem cell proliferation (Buchon et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2011); the role of this system in other muscles may be analogous, controlling expression of various signals to regulate systemic physiology.
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Buchon et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2011).

claim: In mice, early muscle-specific deletion of Growth Hormone Receptor (GHR) causes insulin resistance.
source: In mice, early muscle-specific deletion of Growth Hormone Receptor (GHR) causes several symptoms including insulin resistance, while adult muscle-specific GHR deletion causes entirely different effects, including increased metabolic rate and insulin sensitivity on a high-fat diet (Mavalli et al., 2010; Vijayakumar et al., 2013; Vijayakumar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Mavalli et al., 2010; Vijayakumar et al., 2013; Vijayakumar et al., 2012).

claim: Adult muscle-specific GHR deletion in mice causes increased metabolic rate and insulin sensitivity on a high-fat diet.
source: In mice, early muscle-specific deletion of Growth Hormone Receptor (GHR) causes several symptoms including insulin resistance, while adult muscle-specific GHR deletion causes entirely different effects, including increased metabolic rate and insulin sensitivity on a high-fat diet (Mavalli et al., 2010; Vijayakumar et al., 2013; Vijayakumar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Mavalli et al., 2010; Vijayakumar et al., 2013; Vijayakumar et al., 2012).

claim: STAT5 deletion in adult skeletal muscle promotes muscle lipid accumulation on a high-fat diet.
source: GHR signals via STAT5; STAT5 deletion in adult skeletal muscle promotes muscle lipid accumulation on a high-fat diet (Baik et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Baik et al., 2017).

claim: IL-6 increases skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity when given acutely but can drive insulin resistance when provided chronically.
source: For example, the JAK-STAT activating cytokine IL-6, which signals primarily via STAT3, increases skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity when given acutely but can drive insulin resistance when provided chronically (Nieto-Vazquez et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Nieto-Vazquez et al., 2008).

claim: STAT3 can promote muscle insulin resistance.
source: STAT3 itself can promote muscle insulin resistance (Kim et al., 2013; Mashili et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior research (Kim et al., 2013; Mashili et al., 2013).
